title: Human in the Loop for AI Agents with Step Functions
description:
Human in the loop is my most important safety line as soon as an AI agent stops just writing text and starts doing things that cost money or can’t be undone. A support agent that issues a credit of 5 euros is handy. The same agent refunding 480 euros after a cleverly worded complaint is a problem. Somewhere in between, a person needs to take a quick look.

In the article about the Step Functions AgentCore Gateway I mentioned in passing that approvals don’t belong in the agent’s toolbox. Today I’m building exactly that: a workflow that pauses, asks a human, escalates when nobody answers and only then continues. This time the infrastructure comes entirely from the Serverless Framework.

In short

With the “wait for callback” pattern, Step Functions can wait up to a year for an answer, and the waiting itself costs nothing. You can use it to build approvals for AI agents where the agent can only request an action but never confirm it. The biggest pitfall: the task token works like a master key and belongs neither in emails nor in the hands of the agent.

What you will learn in this article

  • How .waitForTaskToken pauses a workflow and resumes it
  • Why the agent must never have the same permissions as the person who approves
  • How to build deadlines and escalation with TimeoutSeconds and Catch
  • A runnable project with the Serverless Framework, TypeScript and tests

When an AI agent should ask a human

Not every action needs an approval. If you require approval for everything, people will be clicking “yes” on autopilot after three days, and you end up with the effort but without the protection. That’s why I sort actions by two questions: Can it be undone, and how expensive is a mistake?

Suggesting a reply email or checking a status is something the agent may do on its own. The same goes for a small goodwill credit below a fixed limit, as long as it is logged. Anything above that, anything visible to the outside world and anything that deletes data goes through a human. And at the very top there is a limit above which the agent isn’t even allowed to ask.

In the example for this article, a fictional online bookshop runs a support agent. It may request credits. The rules for this don’t live in the prompt but in the workflow:

Amount What happens
up to 20 euros The workflow applies the credit right away, decision “auto”
20.01 to 500 euros The support team must approve; after 4 hours it escalates to the team lead
above 500 euros The workflow stops; the agent isn’t allowed to request this

The difference from the prompt matters. A language model can forget a sentence like “ask before refunding more than 20 euros”, misread it, or be talked out of it through prompt injection. A choice rule in Step Functions can’t be persuaded.

How human in the loop works with Step Functions

Step Functions knows three ways to call a service. Usually the workflow calls something and moves on as soon as the response arrives. If you append .waitForTaskToken to the resource, something else happens: Step Functions creates a task token, hands it to the called service and pauses the step. It only continues once someone calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with exactly this token.

A task token is a long random string that identifies exactly one waiting step. Anyone who knows it and holds the IAM permission states:SendTaskSuccess can complete the step and pass any data as its result. That’s why I treat it like a password.

Waiting is free in Standard workflows. Billing is based on state transitions, according to the pricing page 0.000025 US dollars per transition in us-east-1. So a workflow that waits three days for an approval costs exactly as much as one that continues after three seconds. The upper limit for a single execution is one year. By the way, Express workflows don’t support the callback pattern at all.

🎬 Flow of an approval with Step Functions – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

The flow in the example

  1. The agent calls its “request credit” tool. The tool starts a workflow execution with order number, amount and reason.
  2. A choice rule checks the amount. Small amounts go straight to booking, very large ones stop.
  3. The AskTeam step invokes a Lambda function with .waitForTaskToken. It stores the token in DynamoDB and sends an SNS message that contains only an approval ID.
  4. A person from the team decides. Their request goes, signed, to a second Lambda function, which looks up the token in the table and calls SendTaskSuccess.
  5. If there is no answer within four hours, TimeoutSeconds kicks in. A Catch routes to the AskLead step, which asks the team lead.
  6. If the team lead stays silent too, the workflow sends a final notice and ends with the error ApprovalExpired. Nothing gets booked.

The agent can only start. The workflow handles approval, escalation and expiry.

What matters is what the agent can’t do in this picture. It may start the workflow and read the status of its own executions. It never sees a token, it can’t call the decision function, and SendTaskSuccess doesn’t appear in its role at all.

Step by step: human in the loop with the Serverless Framework

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account in which you may create Lambda, Step Functions, DynamoDB, SNS and IAM roles
  • Node.js 22 or newer and AWS CLI v2 with a working login
  • Serverless Framework v4 (npm i -g serverless); v4 needs a free account or a license key
  • curl 7.75 or newer and jq for the approval script

Step 1: Create the project 

mkdir credit-approval && cd credit-approval
npm init -y
npm i @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb @aws-sdk/client-sfn @aws-sdk/client-sns
npm i -D typescript @types/node @types/aws-lambda vitest aws-sdk-client-mock asl-validator jsonata
mkdir -p src statemachine test scripts

Also set "type": "module" in your package.json. Serverless Framework v4 builds TypeScript handlers with esbuild during deployment, so you don’t need an extra plugin for that.

Step 2: Shared types and input validation

The decision will come from outside later. That’s why I validate it strictly before anything else happens: the approval ID must look like a UUID, the decision is either approved or rejected, and comments get truncated.

// src/approvals.ts
export type Stage = 'team' | 'lead';

export interface CreditRequest {
  orderId: string;
  amountCents: number;
  reason: string;
  requestedBy: string;
}

export interface ApprovalTask {
  taskToken: string;
  stage: Stage;
  executionId: string;
  request: CreditRequest;
}

export interface Decision {
  approvalId: string;
  decision: 'approved' | 'rejected';
  comment?: string;
}

// How long an entry is kept for auditing after the deadline
export const KEEP_SECONDS = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60;

export function parseDecision(body: string | undefined): Decision {
  if (!body) throw new Error('Body is missing');
  const data = JSON.parse(body) as Partial<Decision>;
  if (typeof data.approvalId !== 'string' || !/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/.test(data.approvalId)) {
    throw new Error('approvalId is missing or invalid');
  }
  if (data.decision !== 'approved' && data.decision !== 'rejected') {
    throw new Error('decision must be "approved" or "rejected"');
  }
  const comment = typeof data.comment === 'string' ? data.comment.slice(0, 500) : undefined;
  return { approvalId: data.approvalId, decision: data.decision, comment };
}

export function formatEuro(cents: number): string {
  return new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IE', { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }).format(cents / 100);
}

Step 3: Request the approval

Step Functions invokes this function with the token. It stores the token together with the request and sends a message to the team. Note the attribute_not_exists condition: it prevents a second call from overwriting an entry.

// src/request-approval.ts
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { DynamoDBClient } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';
import { SNSClient, PublishCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-sns';
import { type ApprovalTask, KEEP_SECONDS, formatEuro } from './approvals.js';

const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({}));
const sns = new SNSClient({});

export const handler = async (event: ApprovalTask): Promise<{ approvalId: string }> => {
  const approvalId = randomUUID();
  const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);

  // The task token stays in DynamoDB. The message only contains the approvalId.
  await db.send(new PutCommand({
    TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME,
    Item: {
      approvalId,
      taskToken: event.taskToken,
      stage: event.stage,
      executionId: event.executionId,
      request: event.request,
      status: 'PENDING',
      createdAt: new Date(now * 1000).toISOString(),
      expiresAt: now + KEEP_SECONDS,
    },
    ConditionExpression: 'attribute_not_exists(approvalId)',
  }));

  const { orderId, amountCents, reason, requestedBy } = event.request;
  await sns.send(new PublishCommand({
    TopicArn: process.env.TOPIC_ARN,
    Subject: `Approval needed: credit of ${formatEuro(amountCents)} for ${orderId}`,
    Message: [
      `The support agent (${requestedBy}) wants to issue a credit.`,
      `Order: ${orderId}`,
      `Amount: ${formatEuro(amountCents)}`,
      `Reason: ${reason}`,
      `Stage: ${event.stage === 'team' ? 'Team' : 'Team lead (escalation)'}`,
      '',
      `Approval ID: ${approvalId}`,
      'Decide with: ./decide.sh <approval ID> approved|rejected "comment"',
    ].join('\n'),
    MessageAttributes: { stage: { DataType: 'String', StringValue: event.stage } },
  }));

  return { approvalId };
};

Why not just put the token into a link, as many examples do? Because emails get forwarded, sit in mailboxes and show up in the logs of mail gateways. An approval ID on its own is useless to anyone. The token stays in the table, and only the decision function may read it.

Step 4: Receive the decision

This is the heart of the pattern. The function sits behind a function URL with AWS_IAM authentication. Every request must therefore be signed with valid AWS credentials, and Lambda tells you in the event who signed it. I use that for three checks.

// src/decide.ts
import { DynamoDBClient, ConditionalCheckFailedException } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, GetCommand, UpdateCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';
import { SFNClient, SendTaskSuccessCommand, TaskTimedOut, InvalidToken } from '@aws-sdk/client-sfn';
import type { APIGatewayProxyResultV2, LambdaFunctionURLEventWithIAMAuthorizer } from 'aws-lambda';
import { parseDecision } from './approvals.js';

const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({}));
const sfn = new SFNClient({});

const reply = (statusCode: number, body: object): APIGatewayProxyResultV2 => ({
  statusCode,
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify(body),
});

export const handler = async (event: LambdaFunctionURLEventWithIAMAuthorizer): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResultV2> => {
  // With AuthType AWS_IAM, this tells you who signed the request
  const decidedBy = event.requestContext.authorizer?.iam?.userArn;
  if (!decidedBy) return reply(403, { message: 'IAM signature required' });

  let input;
  try {
    input = parseDecision(event.isBase64Encoded && event.body
      ? Buffer.from(event.body, 'base64').toString('utf8')
      : event.body);
  } catch (error) {
    return reply(400, { message: (error as Error).message });
  }

  const table = process.env.TABLE_NAME;
  const { Item } = await db.send(new GetCommand({ TableName: table, Key: { approvalId: input.approvalId } }));
  if (!Item) return reply(404, { message: 'Approval not found' });

  // Four-eyes principle: whoever requested the credit must not approve it
  if (decidedBy === Item.request.requestedBy) {
    return reply(403, { message: 'You cannot approve your own request' });
  }

  // Only one decision per approval: the first click wins
  try {
    await db.send(new UpdateCommand({
      TableName: table,
      Key: { approvalId: input.approvalId },
      UpdateExpression: 'SET #s = :decided, decidedBy = :by, decidedAt = :at',
      ConditionExpression: '#s = :pending',
      ExpressionAttributeNames: { '#s': 'status' },
      ExpressionAttributeValues: {
        ':decided': input.decision.toUpperCase(),
        ':pending': 'PENDING',
        ':by': decidedBy,
        ':at': new Date().toISOString(),
      },
    }));
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof ConditionalCheckFailedException) {
      return reply(409, { message: 'Someone has already decided' });
    }
    throw error;
  }

  try {
    await sfn.send(new SendTaskSuccessCommand({
      taskToken: Item.taskToken,
      output: JSON.stringify({ decision: input.decision, decidedBy, comment: input.comment ?? '' }),
    }));
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof TaskTimedOut || error instanceof InvalidToken) {
      // Deadline passed or workflow already moved on (e.g. escalated)
      await db.send(new UpdateCommand({
        TableName: table,
        Key: { approvalId: input.approvalId },
        UpdateExpression: 'SET #s = :expired',
        ExpressionAttributeNames: { '#s': 'status' },
        ExpressionAttributeValues: { ':expired': 'EXPIRED' },
      }));
      return reply(410, { message: 'The deadline for this approval has passed' });
    }
    throw error;
  }

  return reply(200, { message: `Decision saved: ${input.decision}` });
};

The first check is the four-eyes principle: whoever requested the credit must not approve it. The second is a conditional update in DynamoDB. If two people click at the same moment, the first one wins and the second gets a 409. The third check deals with expired deadlines. If the step has already timed out and escalated, Step Functions answers with TaskTimedOut. The function then marks the entry as expired and returns a 410.

For the four-eyes principle to work, requestedBy has to be set by the code of the agent tool, for example from the role the tool runs with. If you let the language model fill in this value itself, the check is worthless.

Step 5: Apply the credit

In the example, applying the credit is a placeholder. One detail is still worth it: the credit key is derived from order number and amount. If Step Functions retries the step after an error, no duplicate credit is created, provided your accounting system uses the key as an idempotency key.

// src/apply-credit.ts
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import type { CreditRequest } from './approvals.js';

interface ApplyCreditEvent {
  request: CreditRequest;
  approval: { decision: string; decidedBy: string; comment?: string };
}

export const handler = async (event: ApplyCreditEvent) => {
  // Placeholder for your accounting system. The key makes retries idempotent.
  const creditId = createHash('sha256')
    .update(`${event.request.orderId}:${event.request.amountCents}`)
    .digest('hex')
    .slice(0, 16);

  console.log(JSON.stringify({ msg: 'Credit applied', creditId, ...event }));
  return { status: 'credited', creditId, orderId: event.request.orderId, approvedBy: event.approval.decidedBy };
};

Step 6: The workflow in JSONata

I write the workflow in the JSONata query language. It’s the newer of the two options in Step Functions and reads much more pleasantly than the old path expressions with .$. You get the token via $states.context.Task.Token. With Assign I keep the original request and the decision in variables that are available in all later steps.

{
  "Comment": "Credit requested by an AI agent with human approval and escalation",
  "QueryLanguage": "JSONata",
  "StartAt": "Init",
  "States": {
    "Init": {
      "Type": "Pass",
      "Assign": { "request": "{% $states.input %}" },
      "Next": "CheckAmount"
    },
    "CheckAmount": {
      "Type": "Choice",
      "Choices": [
        { "Condition": "{% $request.amountCents > 50000 %}", "Next": "AboveAgentLimit" },
        {
          "Condition": "{% $request.amountCents <= 2000 %}",
          "Assign": { "approval": { "decision": "approved", "decidedBy": "auto", "comment": "below the approval threshold" } },
          "Next": "ApplyCredit"
        }
      ],
      "Default": "AskTeam"
    },
    "AskTeam": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke.waitForTaskToken",
      "Arguments": {
        "FunctionName": "${RequestApprovalArn}",
        "Payload": {
          "taskToken": "{% $states.context.Task.Token %}",
          "stage": "team",
          "executionId": "{% $states.context.Execution.Id %}",
          "request": "{% $request %}"
        }
      },
      "TimeoutSeconds": 14400,
      "Assign": { "approval": "{% $states.result %}" },
      "Retry": [
        {
          "ErrorEquals": ["Lambda.ServiceException", "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException", "Lambda.SdkClientException"],
          "IntervalSeconds": 2,
          "MaxAttempts": 3,
          "BackoffRate": 2,
          "JitterStrategy": "FULL"
        }
      ],
      "Catch": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.Timeout"], "Next": "AskLead" }],
      "Next": "CheckDecision"
    },
    "AskLead": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke.waitForTaskToken",
      "Arguments": {
        "FunctionName": "${RequestApprovalArn}",
        "Payload": {
          "taskToken": "{% $states.context.Task.Token %}",
          "stage": "lead",
          "executionId": "{% $states.context.Execution.Id %}",
          "request": "{% $request %}"
        }
      },
      "TimeoutSeconds": 72000,
      "Assign": { "approval": "{% $states.result %}" },
      "Retry": [
        {
          "ErrorEquals": ["Lambda.ServiceException", "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException", "Lambda.SdkClientException"],
          "IntervalSeconds": 2,
          "MaxAttempts": 3,
          "BackoffRate": 2,
          "JitterStrategy": "FULL"
        }
      ],
      "Catch": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.Timeout"], "Next": "NotifyExpired" }],
      "Next": "CheckDecision"
    },
    "CheckDecision": {
      "Type": "Choice",
      "Choices": [{ "Condition": "{% $approval.decision = 'approved' %}", "Next": "ApplyCredit" }],
      "Default": "Rejected"
    },
    "ApplyCredit": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Arguments": {
        "FunctionName": "${ApplyCreditArn}",
        "Payload": { "request": "{% $request %}", "approval": "{% $approval %}" }
      },
      "Output": "{% $states.result.Payload %}",
      "Retry": [
        {
          "ErrorEquals": ["Lambda.ServiceException", "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException", "Lambda.SdkClientException"],
          "IntervalSeconds": 2,
          "MaxAttempts": 3,
          "BackoffRate": 2,
          "JitterStrategy": "FULL"
        }
      ],
      "End": true
    },
    "Rejected": {
      "Type": "Succeed",
      "Output": {
        "status": "rejected",
        "orderId": "{% $request.orderId %}",
        "decidedBy": "{% $approval.decidedBy %}",
        "comment": "{% $approval.comment %}"
      }
    },
    "NotifyExpired": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::sns:publish",
      "Arguments": {
        "TopicArn": "${TopicArn}",
        "Subject": "Approval expired",
        "Message": "{% 'Nobody decided on order ' & $request.orderId & ' in time. No credit was applied.' %}"
      },
      "Next": "Expired"
    },
    "Expired": {
      "Type": "Fail",
      "Error": "ApprovalExpired",
      "Cause": "Nobody decided within the deadline."
    },
    "AboveAgentLimit": {
      "Type": "Fail",
      "Error": "AmountAboveAgentLimit",
      "Cause": "The agent must not request credits above 500 euros."
    }
  }
}

Take a closer look at three spots. TimeoutSeconds in the AskTeam step is set to 14,400 seconds, which is four hours. You don’t need HeartbeatSeconds here, because humans don’t send signs of life. The Catch handles States.Timeout and passes the request one level up. Finally, CloudFormation replaces placeholders such as ${RequestApprovalArn} at deployment time via DefinitionSubstitutions.

The Retry rule on the approval steps only repeats real Lambda failures. Each retry creates a new token and therefore a new approval ID. That’s intended; the old ID then leads to a 410.

Step 7: Infrastructure with the Serverless Framework

The Serverless Framework describes the Lambda functions as usual. I create the workflow as a regular CloudFormation resource under resources and load the definition with ${file(...)}. This way I don’t need an additional plugin, and the file stays the same one I validate locally.

# serverless.yml
service: credit-approval

provider:
  name: aws
  runtime: nodejs24.x
  region: eu-central-1
  architecture: arm64
  memorySize: 256
  timeout: 10
  environment:
    TABLE_NAME: !Ref ApprovalsTable
    TOPIC_ARN: !Ref ApprovalTopic
  iam:
    role:
      statements:
        - Effect: Allow
          Action: dynamodb:PutItem
          Resource: !GetAtt ApprovalsTable.Arn
        - Effect: Allow
          Action: sns:Publish
          Resource: !Ref ApprovalTopic

functions:
  requestApproval:
    handler: src/request-approval.handler

  decide:
    handler: src/decide.handler
    # Separate role: only this function may resume workflows
    role: DecideRole
    url:
      authorizer: aws_iam

  applyCredit:
    handler: src/apply-credit.handler

resources:
  Resources:
    ApprovalsTable:
      Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
      Properties:
        BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
        AttributeDefinitions:
          - AttributeName: approvalId
            AttributeType: S
        KeySchema:
          - AttributeName: approvalId
            KeyType: HASH
        TimeToLiveSpecification:
          AttributeName: expiresAt
          Enabled: true
        PointInTimeRecoverySpecification:
          PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled: true

    ApprovalTopic:
      Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
      Properties:
        DisplayName: Credit approvals

    ApproverEmail:
      Type: AWS::SNS::Subscription
      Properties:
        TopicArn: !Ref ApprovalTopic
        Protocol: email
        Endpoint: ${param:approverEmail}

    DecideRole:
      Type: AWS::IAM::Role
      Properties:
        AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
          Version: '2012-10-17'
          Statement:
            - Effect: Allow
              Principal:
                Service: lambda.amazonaws.com
              Action: sts:AssumeRole
        ManagedPolicyArns:
          - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole'
        Policies:
          - PolicyName: decide
            PolicyDocument:
              Version: '2012-10-17'
              Statement:
                - Effect: Allow
                  Action:
                    - dynamodb:GetItem
                    - dynamodb:UpdateItem
                  Resource: !GetAtt ApprovalsTable.Arn
                - Effect: Allow
                  # SendTaskSuccess cannot be scoped to a resource
                  Action: states:SendTaskSuccess
                  Resource: '*'

    CreditApprovalRole:
      Type: AWS::IAM::Role
      Properties:
        AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
          Version: '2012-10-17'
          Statement:
            - Effect: Allow
              Principal:
                Service: states.amazonaws.com
              Action: sts:AssumeRole
        Policies:
          - PolicyName: credit-approval
            PolicyDocument:
              Version: '2012-10-17'
              Statement:
                - Effect: Allow
                  Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
                  Resource:
                    - !GetAtt RequestApprovalLambdaFunction.Arn
                    - !GetAtt ApplyCreditLambdaFunction.Arn
                - Effect: Allow
                  Action: sns:Publish
                  Resource: !Ref ApprovalTopic

    CreditApprovalStateMachine:
      Type: AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine
      Properties:
        StateMachineType: STANDARD
        RoleArn: !GetAtt CreditApprovalRole.Arn
        Definition: ${file(./statemachine/credit-approval.asl.json)}
        DefinitionSubstitutions:
          RequestApprovalArn: !GetAtt RequestApprovalLambdaFunction.Arn
          ApplyCreditArn: !GetAtt ApplyCreditLambdaFunction.Arn
          TopicArn: !Ref ApprovalTopic

    # Attach this policy to the role of the people allowed to approve
    ApproverPolicy:
      Type: AWS::IAM::ManagedPolicy
      Properties:
        Description: Can approve or reject credits
        PolicyDocument:
          Version: '2012-10-17'
          Statement:
            - Effect: Allow
              Action: lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl
              Resource: !GetAtt DecideLambdaFunction.Arn
              Condition:
                StringEquals:
                  lambda:FunctionUrlAuthType: AWS_IAM
            - Effect: Allow
              Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
              Resource: !GetAtt DecideLambdaFunction.Arn
              Condition:
                Bool:
                  lambda:InvokedViaFunctionUrl: 'true'

    # And this one to the AI agent's role: start and read status, nothing else
    AgentPolicy:
      Type: AWS::IAM::ManagedPolicy
      Properties:
        Description: Can start credit requests and read their status
        PolicyDocument:
          Version: '2012-10-17'
          Statement:
            - Effect: Allow
              Action: states:StartExecution
              Resource: !Ref CreditApprovalStateMachine
            - Effect: Allow
              Action: states:DescribeExecution
              Resource: !Sub
                - 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:states:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:execution:${Name}:*'
                - Name: !GetAtt CreditApprovalStateMachine.Name

  Outputs:
    StateMachineArn:
      Value: !Ref CreditApprovalStateMachine
    ApproverPolicyArn:
      Value: !Ref ApproverPolicy
    AgentPolicyArn:
      Value: !Ref AgentPolicy

A few decisions in this file are deliberate. The decide function gets its own role because it’s the only one that needs states:SendTaskSuccess. This action can’t be scoped to a specific workflow in IAM, so I keep the circle of those who have it as small as possible. The two managed policies at the end are meant for humans and agent: attach ApproverPolicy to the approvers’ role and AgentPolicy to the role the agent tool runs with.

For function URLs with AWS_IAM, Lambda now requires two permissions: lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction. I restrict the second one with the condition lambda:InvokedViaFunctionUrl so nobody can call the function while bypassing the URL.

Step 8: The approval script

To get started, a small script is enough for someone on the team to decide. It fetches the credentials of the current session and signs the request with curl’s SigV4 support.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/decide.sh – send a signed decision to the function URL
# Usage: ./scripts/decide.sh <approval ID> approved|rejected "comment"
set -euo pipefail

: "${DECIDE_URL:?Please set DECIDE_URL to the function URL}"
REGION="${AWS_REGION:-eu-central-1}"

# Gets the credentials of your current session (AWS CLI v2)
eval "$(aws configure export-credentials --format env)"

BODY=$(jq -n --arg id "$1" --arg d "$2" --arg c "${3:-}" \
  '{approvalId: $id, decision: $d, comment: $c}')

TOKEN_HEADER=()
if [ -n "${AWS_SESSION_TOKEN:-}" ]; then
  TOKEN_HEADER=(-H "x-amz-security-token: ${AWS_SESSION_TOKEN}")
fi

curl --fail-with-body -sS "$DECIDE_URL" \
  --aws-sigv4 "aws:amz:${REGION}:lambda" \
  --user "${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}:${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}" \
  "${TOKEN_HEADER[@]}" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d "$BODY"
echo

Later you can put the same thing behind a button in Slack or Teams. What matters is that the application behind the button checks the identity of the person clicking and passes it on as decidedBy.

Step 9: Test, deploy, try it out

The tests check the decision function with mocked AWS clients and evaluate the workflow’s choice rules with the jsonata library. You’ll find the complete test files in the repository at the end of this article.

npx tsc --noEmit
npx asl-validator --json-path statemachine/credit-approval.asl.json
npx vitest run
serverless deploy --param="approverEmail=support-team@example.com"

Expected result: ten green tests, a valid state machine definition and, after deployment, three outputs with the ARNs of the workflow and the policies. Then confirm the SNS subscription email, otherwise no approval request will arrive.

Now start a credit request the way the agent’s tool would:

aws stepfunctions start-execution \
  --state-machine-arn "<StateMachineArn from the outputs>" \
  --input '{"orderId":"B-1001","amountCents":4500,"reason":"Book delivered with water damage","requestedBy":"arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/support-agent/session-1"}'

In the console, the execution now sits in the AskTeam step. Use the approval ID from the email to decide:

export DECIDE_URL="<function URL of decide>"
./scripts/decide.sh 7f1c2d3e-4b5a-4c6d-8e9f-0a1b2c3d4e5f approved "Photo of the damage provided"

The response is {"message":"Decision saved: approved"}, and the execution continues to ApplyCredit. Run the same command again and you’ll get a 409.

Common mistakes with human in the loop

The token in the link. Many tutorials attach the task token to an approval link as a query parameter. It works, but it hands a key to every system that sees the email. A short ID plus a lookup in the table costs you ten lines of code.

The agent can approve itself. If the agent tool also gets SendTaskSuccess, the whole setup is theatre. Review the agent’s role regularly, ideally automated with IAM Access Analyzer or a test against the policy.

No deadline. Without TimeoutSeconds, a step waits until the one-year limit. Nobody notices that an approval is sitting in the inbox of a colleague who is on vacation. Always set a deadline and think about what should happen afterwards.

Treating rejection as an error. I deliberately return rejections via SendTaskSuccess with decision: rejected. I would only use SendTaskFailure for technical problems; otherwise business decisions end up in your error alarms.

Too many approvals. When the team gets fifty requests a day, people stop reading and start clicking. After two weeks, check how often requests were rejected. If the rate is close to zero, your threshold is probably too low.

Costs and security

Costs are rarely the issue with this pattern. An execution with an approval has around a dozen state transitions, plus three short Lambda invocations, two DynamoDB writes and one SNS message. Even a thousand credits a month stay in the range of cents to a few euros. The waiting itself is free.

Security deserves a second look. The table with the tokens is the most sensitive piece of the architecture, so don’t grant any other function access to it. Keep the TTL attribute enabled so old entries disappear; I described how that works in detail in the article on DynamoDB TTL. And log every decision with decidedBy so you can trace later who approved what.

If you’re not sure whether Step Functions is the right tool for your case at all, the AWS service finder helps you decide.

My take

I don’t see human in the loop as a sign of distrust towards AI. It’s the same logic we have applied to people for years: new colleagues can’t refund 500 euros on their first day either. Trust grows with experience, and an approval threshold is a dial you can turn up later.

What I’m critical of is the temptation to handle approvals in the prompt. “Ask the user before you do anything important” is a request, not a control. The control belongs in a layer the model can’t influence. Step Functions works well for that, because the flow is visible, versioned and understandable in the console for everyone, including people from the business side who never read a line of TypeScript.

The pattern does have a catch: it slows processes down. The agent can no longer tell the customer right away that the money is on its way. I think that’s an honest price. In that case the agent should say that the credit is being reviewed, rather than promise something nobody has decided yet.

FAQ

What does human in the loop mean for AI agents?

A person reviews certain actions of the agent before they are carried out. The agent proposes, a human decides, and only then does the action continue.

How long can Step Functions wait for an approval?

A Standard workflow can run for up to one year and wait that long for a task token. In practice, you should set a much shorter deadline with TimeoutSeconds.

Does waiting for an approval cost money?

No. Standard workflows are billed by state transitions, not by runtime. A waiting step doesn’t cause any additional costs.

Does waitForTaskToken work with Express workflows?

No. Express workflows only support direct request-response calls. For approvals you need a Standard workflow.

Your next step

Look at the tools your agent has today and mark every one that moves money, deletes data or sends something to the outside world. Exactly these tools are worth an approval workflow. Start with a low threshold and measure how often someone actually steps in.

I’d like to know where you draw the line: Do you let your agents move money at all, or is that off-limits for you? Let me know in the comments.

Continue the series: Go to the overview “Serverless patterns in practice” · Previous part: Receiving webhooks with Lambda: signatures, duplicates, SQS

Sources

  • AWS Step Functions: service integration patterns (wait for callback with task token)
  • AWS Step Functions API: SendTaskSuccess
  • AWS Step Functions: Context object in JSONata and JSONPath
  • AWS Step Functions: pricing
  • AWS Lambda: Control access to function URLs
  • AWS Compute Blog: security incident response with Step Functions (callback pattern)

This post was created with AI assistance.

title: ChatGPT Updates by OpenAI in October 2026: New Features, AI Tools, and Business Benefits
description:
Artificial intelligence continues to change how businesses create content, analyze information, develop software, and manage everyday tasks. OpenAI is advancing this transformation with regular improvements to ChatGPT, introducing features that make AI more interactive, practical, and useful for professional work.

The ChatGPT updates of October 2026 include GPT-6 with Intelligent UI, audio file uploads, collaborative presentation creation, enhanced reasoning capabilities, and new integrations with productivity tools. These developments offer businesses new ways to improve efficiency, support employees, and simplify digital workflows.

For organizations exploring AI adoption, understanding the latest OpenAI ChatGPT updates can help identify opportunities to improve productivity and prepare for the next stage of digital transformation.

1. GPT-6 Introduces Intelligent UI in ChatGPT

One of the major ChatGPT updates in October 2026 is the introduction of GPT-6 with Intelligent UI, announced on October 7. This feature allows ChatGPT to present information using a combination of text, visuals, interactive elements, and useful tools.

Instead of providing only traditional text responses, ChatGPT can generate interactive calculators, diagrams, comparison layouts, and other experiences based on the user's request. It can also begin answering while continuing to process information or use tools.

These capabilities make AI assistance more adaptable to different tasks.

How businesses can benefit

  • Marketing: Organize campaign ideas, compare strategies, and explore marketing performance.
  • Software development: Understand technical concepts and review information through structured visual explanations.
  • Business analysis: Present comparisons and explore figures using interactive tools.
  • Customer support: Make complex information easier for customers to understand. The availability of these features depends on the ChatGPT plan, model selection, and rollout status. Businesses can explore how interactive AI experiences fit into their existing processes.

2. GPT-6.1 Terra Improves AI-Assisted Work

On October 26, OpenAI announced the rollout of GPT-6.1 Terra in ChatGPT Work and Codex. The model supports tasks involving visual reasoning, computer use, and writing.

GPT-6.1 Terra is designed to help users handle practical work such as interpreting technical drawings, drafting proposals, working with forms, and completing computer-based tasks.

For businesses, these capabilities demonstrate how AI is moving beyond simple question-and-answer interactions toward assistance with more complex workflows.

Potential applications of GPT-6.1 Terra

  • Preparing business documents and proposals.
  • Interpreting visual and technical information.
  • Supporting software development workflows.
  • Assisting with repetitive computer-based activities.
  • Improving the preparation and organization of business information. GPT-6.1 Terra is rolling out to eligible Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users in supported ChatGPT Work and Codex experiences. Access may vary according to account eligibility and workspace settings.

3. ChatGPT Slides Supports Presentation Creation and Collaboration

Another important development arrived on October 16 with the introduction of ChatGPT Slides.

This feature allows eligible users to create and refine presentations using a conversation, uploaded files, an outline, or an example presentation. Users can edit text, images, shapes, and charts, as well as request changes through natural-language instructions.

ChatGPT Slides also supports team collaboration, including real-time editing and shared comments in Space. Users can present their work directly or export presentations into supported formats.

Why ChatGPT Slides matters for businesses

Creating presentations can take considerable time, particularly when teams need to organize research, prepare visual content, and revise slides repeatedly.

ChatGPT Slides can help businesses:

Create initial presentation drafts more efficiently.
Organize reports into structured slide decks.
Refine presentation layouts and visual elements.
Collaborate with colleagues on shared presentations.
Prepare business proposals, marketing plans, and project updates.
The feature is rolling out to eligible Pro, Business, and Enterprise users with Space access. Its availability depends on the user's plan and supported environment.

4. Audio Uploads Make Meetings and Recordings Easier to Analyze

OpenAI introduced audio uploads in ChatGPT on October 6. Eligible paid subscribers and workspaces can upload supported audio files to generate transcripts, summarize recordings, and ask questions about their contents.

This feature can help professionals convert recorded conversations into more useful business information.

For example, a company can use an eligible audio upload workflow to summarize a recorded meeting, identify key discussion points, organize action items, or prepare a follow-up email draft.

Business applications of ChatGPT audio uploads

  • Meeting management: Turn recordings into structured meeting notes.
  • Human resources: Organize interview recordings and discussion summaries where appropriate and authorized.
  • Content creation: Develop written material from recorded interviews.
  • Research: Summarize lectures, discussions, and recorded research sessions.
  • Project management: Extract decisions and follow-up tasks from meetings. Audio transcription may contain errors, and performance can vary by language, audio quality, and recording conditions. Businesses should review transcripts before using them for important decisions and obtain appropriate permission before processing recordings.

5. GPT-6 Pro Receives Improvements for Complex Tasks

On October 16, OpenAI also announced improvements to GPT-6 Pro in the ChatGPT chat experience for eligible users.

The update includes faster responses, improved use of plugins and tools, and support for multiple agents working on different parts of a task in parallel. Users can follow the agents' progress and review their completed work.

This approach can be valuable when a task involves several related activities rather than a single question.

For example, a marketing team might use AI assistance to research a topic, organize findings, develop a content outline, and prepare a draft for human review. Parallel task execution can help organize complex work, although results still require appropriate verification.

For businesses, the key opportunity is to identify tasks that benefit from structured AI assistance while maintaining human oversight over final decisions and published content.

6. ChatGPT Connects with More Productivity Tools

OpenAI's October 2026 release notes also include an update for iCloud users. On October 27, iCloud Mail and Calendar connections became available in ChatGPT on the web, desktop app, and iOS across ChatGPT plans.

With these connections, users can ask ChatGPT to find emails, catch up on inbox activity, check their schedules, and update calendar events.

Connected applications can make AI assistance more useful because users can work with relevant information without repeatedly switching between different tools.

What this means for organizations
Businesses are increasingly looking for ways to connect AI with their existing productivity systems. Integrations can help employees organize communications, prepare for meetings, and manage schedules more efficiently.

However, users should review the permissions granted to connected applications and ensure that sensitive business information is handled according to organizational policies.

Availability of individual integrations and actions may vary by platform, region, account permissions, and rollout status.

7. Locked Chats Add Another Privacy Option

On October 20, OpenAI introduced locked chats, allowing eligible users to hide selected conversations from regular chat history, pinned chats, and search.

Locked chats can be opened using an account PIN or supported device authentication. The feature is rolling out gradually across supported plans and platforms.

This addition offers users another way to control the visibility of selected conversations within their ChatGPT account.

However, locking a conversation should not be confused with deleting it or changing its data-retention settings. Organizations handling confidential information should continue following their established security, privacy, and data-management requirements.

How Businesses Can Use the Latest ChatGPT Features

The October 2026 ChatGPT updates highlight several opportunities for businesses adopting artificial intelligence.

Improve content production: Use AI to develop outlines, organize research, prepare presentation drafts, and refine marketing materials.

Simplify information management: Summarize eligible recordings, organize meeting notes, and extract key information from documents.

Support digital transformation: Evaluate AI-assisted workflows that reduce repetitive work and help employees focus on higher-value activities.

Enhance software development: Explore AI tools for coding, technical analysis, and other development tasks supported by the selected model and platform.

Strengthen productivity: Assess whether connected applications and interactive AI tools can simplify routine business processes.

Successful AI adoption requires more than access to new features. Companies should establish clear usage policies, protect sensitive information, verify AI-generated outputs, and measure the results of their AI initiatives.

Conclusion

The ChatGPT updates of October 2026 demonstrate OpenAI's continued focus on making artificial intelligence more useful for everyday work. GPT-6 Intelligent UI, GPT-6.1 Terra, ChatGPT Slides, audio uploads, improved multi-agent capabilities, and productivity integrations offer new possibilities for businesses and professionals.

For companies planning their digital transformation strategies, these developments provide useful examples of how AI can support content creation, information management, collaboration, and software development.

At Allianze, businesses can explore how AI and modern technology solutions align with their digital goals. Evaluating suitable tools, identifying practical use cases, and implementing responsible AI workflows can help organizations make informed decisions as artificial intelligence continues to evolve.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What are the major ChatGPT updates in October 2026?
Major updates include GPT-6 with Intelligent UI, GPT-6.1 Terra in ChatGPT Work and Codex, ChatGPT Slides, audio file uploads, improved GPT-6 Pro capabilities, iCloud Mail and Calendar connections, and locked chats.

2. What is GPT-6 Intelligent UI?
GPT-6 Intelligent UI enables ChatGPT to combine text with visual and interactive elements, such as diagrams, comparison layouts, and task-specific tools, depending on the user's request.

3. Can ChatGPT create business presentations in October 2026?
Yes. ChatGPT Slides supports presentation creation, editing, collaboration, and exporting for eligible users. Availability depends on the user's subscription and workspace access.

4. How can businesses use ChatGPT for productivity?
Businesses can explore ChatGPT for research, content drafting, meeting summaries, presentation creation, software development assistance, and selected workflows involving connected applications.

5. Are all new ChatGPT features available to every user?
No. Availability varies by subscription, region, platform, workspace settings, and rollout status. Users should consult OpenAI's official release notes for the latest eligibility details.

6. Why should businesses follow OpenAI ChatGPT updates?
Following OpenAI updates helps businesses evaluate emerging AI capabilities, identify potential workflow improvements, understand feature limitations, and make informed decisions about AI adoption.
